summary: This informational RFC creates an IANA registry for Content Security Policy directives. It fills the registry with the directives defined in the Content Security Policy Level 2 specification, so that new directives can be tracked in one place.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC creates an official list of Content Security Policy directives, the named rules that control what a web page can use. Each new directive must have a public specification explaining how it works.

subtitle: How Content Security Policy directives are documented and registered.

tldr.problem: Content Security Policy uses named directives, so people need a public record of those names and their meaning.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7762 creates an IANA registry and requires new and updated directives to be registered with a public specification.
tldr.outcome: A designated expert reviews registrations under the Specification Required policy.

today: RFC 7762 is an Informational RFC from January 2016. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why CSP Directives Need a Registry
sections.content:
Content Security Policy (CSP) lets web developers control which resources a page can fetch or execute, along with other security-related choices. Its policy language is an extensible set of directives, each controlling a resource type or policy choice.

RFC 7762 establishes a registry so extensions can be listed and standardized.
sections.plainLanguage: CSP uses named rules to control what a web page can load or run. This RFC creates an official list so people can look up the rules and add new ones in a consistent way.

sections.title: What a Directive Specification Must Say
sections.content:
A directive must be described in a readily available public specification. The specification MUST explain its syntax, intended use and meaning fully, to support independent implementations and prevent accidental name collisions.

Documents that define new CSP directives MUST register them with IANA. A registration gives the directive name and a reference to its specification. The name is an ASCII string made from letters, digits and hyphens, with at least one character.
sections.plainLanguage: A new directive needs a public document that explains exactly how it is written and what it means. Its authors must register its name and link that explanation in the IANA list.

sections.title: Review Policy and Starting Entries
sections.content:
The registry uses the Specification Required policy, which means a designated expert reviews the specification. The IESG SHOULD draw experts from the W3C security community through its liaison.

The expert should consider whether a proposed directive undermines CSP's restrictive security role. The review should also balance useful fine-grained controls against adding controls without known security implications. The initial registry contains the directives defined by the CSP Level 2 specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A designated expert checks each proposed rule against its public specification. The expert considers whether the rule fits CSP's goal of restricting page behavior and whether its security effect is understood.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Documentation
sections.content:
The registry itself has no security implications, but CSP directives do. A specification for a new directive MUST include detailed security and privacy considerations.

The specification SHOULD also explain expected implementation and usage so web developers can understand how the directive is meant to work.
sections.plainLanguage: The list does not create a security risk by itself. Each rule can affect security and privacy, so its specification must explain those effects and should describe how developers are expected to use it.
